display_title: Interesting idea for Gaussian distribution case

content.title: Interesting idea for Gaussian distribution case
content.review:
### **Summary and Contributions of Paper**
This paper proposes a new method (CoNES) to compute a relaxed version of the Natural Gradient, via convex programming due to the convexity of the relaxed problem when using Gaussian distribution parameterizations. Experiments comparing CoNES with ES, NES, and CMA with are shown on standard blackbox functions as well as Mujoco benchmarks.

### **Strengths**
- The writing quality is clear and understandable for a broad set of readers.
- The approach is novel and theoretically sound. 
- Tackles second-order optimization in ES problems, an under-studied case.

### **Weaknesses**
- In the experimental section, the Adam Optimizer is used, which can confound the results. In general, it is uncommon to do this with ES techniques, and I'm not sure if, for instance, CoNES is better only when in combination with the Adam Optimizer (unlikely, but can be a possibility). It would be better if the authors used raw gradient descent in the experimental section.
- Experiments could be stronger for the RL case. Right now, there's not a large improvement for the Mujoco benchmarks, while it can be complicated to implement CoNES due to the convex programming solver. Part of the reason seems to be that NES does not highly boost performance on these benchmarks. I suggest certain modifications to these benchmarks to see if NES/CoNES works better, such as: 1. Projecting the parameter space to higher dimensions using a random orthogonal matrix (which is also a reparameterization of the search space, to test parametrization invariance), 2. Stacking more Tanh layers in the policy, which would justify the claim about natural gradients avoiding vanishing gradients due to Tanh.
- It would be good if the authors could also provide some sort of study (theoretical or empirical ablation) on how much the CoNES gradient matches with the true natural gradient, compared to using an estimate of the natural gradient, given the same number of perturbations used for both cases. This is especially true since the authors state that they use the same hyperparameters for all methods (ES, CoNES, NES), which means that the quality of the optimization method is most likely dependent on the quality/variance of the natural gradient estimation.

Overall, I think the submission is fine but could be polished more, and thus my score is marginally above the acceptance threshold.
If the authors could fix the mentioned weaknesses, I would be happy to raise my score.

### **Clarity Remarks**
- Can you please clarify how you're computing the NES benchmark? e.g. is it Algorithm 3 from (https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume15/wierstra14a/wierstra14a.pdf)?
- It would be better to not use \delta\theta to describe the perturbation, since \theta is already vector with a fixed direction, while the intention is to convey that \delta\theta can be any direction within a ball.

content.title: Author Response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their insightful and constructive comments. Below we address the reviewer’s main comments:

**[Q.]** In the experimental section, the Adam Optimizer is used, which can confound the results. In general, it is uncommon to do this with ES techniques, and I'm not sure if, for instance, CoNES is better only when in combination with the Adam Optimizer (unlikely, but can be a possibility). It would be better if the authors used raw gradient descent in the experimental section.

**[A.]** The use of the Adam optimizer with blackbox methods is quite popular. Some papers that do this include:
1. https://arxiv.org/pdf/1703.03864.pdf
2. https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2019/file/88bade49e98db8790df275fcebb37a13-Paper.pdf
3. https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2018/file/b1301141feffabac455e1f90a7de2054-Paper.pdf -- see the ES configurations in their code: https://github.com/uber-research/deep-neuroevolution

**[Q.]** Experiments could be stronger for the RL case. Right now, there's not a large improvement for the Mujoco benchmarks, while it can be complicated to implement CoNES due to the convex programming solver. Part of the reason seems to be that NES does not highly boost performance on these benchmarks. I suggest certain modifications to these benchmarks to see if NES/CoNES works better, such as: 1. Projecting the parameter space to higher dimensions using a random orthogonal matrix (which is also a reparameterization of the search space, to test parametrization invariance), 2. Stacking more Tanh layers in the policy, which would justify the claim about natural gradients avoiding vanishing gradients due to Tanh.

**[A.]** We very much appreciate these constructive suggestions that we will incorporate in the results.

**[Q.]** It would be good if the authors could also provide some sort of study (theoretical or empirical ablation) on how much the CoNES gradient matches with the true natural gradient, compared to using an estimate of the natural gradient, given the same number of perturbations used for both cases.

**[A.]** Theoretically, as the radius of the KL-divergence ball shrinks to 0, the CoNES gradient will converge to the NES gradient; this follows from Remark 1 in the paper. We would be happy to clarify this theoretical outcome in the paper.

**[Q.]** Can you please clarify how you're computing the NES benchmark?

**[A.]** We compute the inverse of the Fisher information matrix analytically and then multiply it with the vanilla ES gradient estimate. The details can be found in the file `es_grad.py`, `method=='eNES_logvar_centered_utility'`, lines 154-174. The code is provided in the supplementary material.

content.title: Many problems, flawed experimental results
content.review:
SUMMARY

This paper proposes a variant of the NES algorithm for convex problems. However, it is based on a gradient estimator that differs significantly from NES, and it solves a problem that has a solution since 10 years.


CRITICISM

The paper cites [Salimans 2017] right next to [Rechenberg 1973]. There are hundreds of better references on ES than the OpenAI paper, for example all the original work on CMA-ES. Indeed, Salimans used a very much reduced algorithm that remotely resembles and ES, even lacking step size control, without making any contribution to ES research. Citing it as an original paper on ES reveals a serious lack of knowledge of the field.

For CMA-ES, the standard reference is:
Hansen, Nikolaus, and Andreas Ostermeier. "Completely derandomized self-adaptation in evolution strategies." Evolutionary computation 9.2 (2001): 159-195.
This paper cites a benchmark study from 2016 instead.

It is claimed in the introduction that NES would need to estimate the Fisher matrix. That is wrong in many ways. First of all, Gaussian distributions are used all the time, and then the matrix is known in analytic form. Second, the xNES implementation of NES provides a neat way of getting around computing the matrix at all:
Glasmachers et al. "Exponential natural evolution strategies." Proceedings of the 12th annual conference on Genetic and evolutionary computation. 2010.

Section 4.2: "This gradient estimate is then supplied to a gradient-based optimizer to update the belief distribution." Wrong. All practical NES implementations rely on ranking of solutions, not on the plain gradient estimator. This is absolutely essential, see
Beyer. "Convergence analysis of evolutionary algorithms that are based on the paradigm of information geometry." Evolutionary Computation 22.4 (2014): 679-709.

First sentence of section 5: "the computationally expensive estimation of the Fisher information matrix $F (\theta)$ and its inverse makes it difficult to scale to very high-dimensional problems." This is a long-solved problem, see [Glasmachers et al., 2010] above.

The paper contains two unsurprising theorems which do not really touch core questions like convergence properties. Therefore the main claim to fame of the proposed method is empirical performance. Sadly, the experiments are not convincing at all.


EXPERIMENTS

I will focus on the results on analytic problems. What I see here is as wrong as it gets. It is obvious that the results are entirely dominated by wrong initial step size settings. They are completely meaningless. I don't know what goes wrong here, but I see only two options: either the authors use bad initial parameters for their competitor methods on purpose, or they don't know how to properly use an ES.

The only way to make a non-elitist ES like CMA-ES get worse on a convex function is to start it with a too large initial step size. This happens on all four analytic problems. It is well known that CMA-ES vastly outperforms NES on sphere due to better step size control. Also, how can the step size of an ES increase on sphere after it already decreased? For all the ES in the field, if properly implemented and properly initialized, the log-distance to the optimum will decay at a fixed multiplicative rate (linear convergence), and so does the step size. This was proven rigorously for the (1+1)-ES, for all convex quadratic problems:
Jägersküpper, Jens. "How the (1+1) ES using isotropic mutations minimizes positive definite quadratic forms." Theoretical Computer Science 361.1 (2006): 38-56.
The same holds true empirically for all ES, including NES and CMA-ES. For all of these reasons the results are entirely implausible and reveal serious problems with the paper. I can only speculate about the reasons. One option is a wrong implementation.

I checked the code. Whatever is referred to here as an ES or a NES algorithm has not much to do with it. I refuse to call these algorithms ES. There is no selection, there is not even any ranking. What I see here are cheaply estimated stochastic (natural) gradients at work. Interestingly, the authors cite the NES paper but apparently ignore its contents; instead they prefer to roll their own reduced algorithm and call it NES. The resulting algorithms do not achieve linear convergence, see [Beyer, 2014] above.

Please ALWAYS plot objective function regrets and step sizes on a log-scale. That will make sense as soon as the ES algorithms are implemented correctly so that linear convergence can be obtained. Refer to figure 3 of the cited NES paper
https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume15/wierstra14a/wierstra14a.pdf
for an example.

Please provide a comparison on the well-established BBOB/COCO benchmark suite, possibly restricted to convex functions. There is no need to rerun competitor algorithms since that data is publicly available:
https://github.com/numbbo/coco


RECOMMENDATION

The papar has far too many weak spots. Some of the experimental results are ridiculous. I strongly recommend to reject the paper.
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

content.title: Author Response: Part 1
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their comments. Below we address the reviewer’s main comments:

**[Q.]** This paper proposes a variant of the NES algorithm for convex problems. 

**[A.]** We would like to clarify that CoNES is not necessarily meant for convex problems. On the contrary, CoNES is formulated to work on non-convex problems. This is demonstrated through the numerical examples in the paper, such as Lunacek, Rastrigin and the reinforcement learning (RL) examples. Also, the theoretical results of the paper, i.e., Theorem 1 and 2, hold for any non-convex loss function.

**[Q.]** However, it is based on a gradient estimator that differs significantly from NES, and it solves a problem that has a solution since 10 years. 

**[A.]** The contribution of CoNES does not lie in its ability to compute the natural gradient efficiently (which has indeed been addressed in prior papers) but rather its ability to tune the direction of the estimated gradient with the step size of the optimizer, as mentioned in the Introduction of the paper: “tuning the radius of the KL-divergence ball facilitates better alignment of the update direction with the update step size, yielding faster convergence than NES (which provides the steepest ascent direction for infinitesimal step lengths).”  This ability to tune the KL-divergence ball endows trust-region-like benefits to NES-like gradient estimates, which has not been thoroughly explored in the literature.

Indeed, due to the importance of the radius of the KL-divergence ball, we provided a literature review on “Trust-regions for blackbox optimization” in Section 2, Related Work. 
We also bring this issue up towards the end of Section 5: “The NES gradient is the sharpest ascent direction for an infinitesimal step size, but it may not be ideal for a larger step size. With CoNES, we can tune the scalar parameter $\epsilon$ to better align the update direction with the gradient-based optimizer’s step size (learning rate), yielding faster updates. Indeed, the choice of $\epsilon$ is important to the performance of CoNES as demonstrated in our numerical results in Section 7.2. The mechanism for selecting (or adapting) the hyperparameter $\epsilon$ is beyond the scope of this paper and will be explored in our future work.” 
In the results, we again point to the importance of the KL-divergence ball: “It is worth pointing out that for RL tasks, CoNES demonstrates high sensitivity to the choice of $\epsilon$. The results for CoNES reported in Fig. 4 and Table 1 are for the best choice of $\epsilon$ from $[\sqrt{0.1},\sqrt{1},\sqrt{10},\sqrt{100},\sqrt{1000}]$.” 
Finally, due to the importance of the choice of the KL-divergence ball’s radius, the first point we raise in our future work is: “The performance of CoNES is dependent on the choice of the radius $\epsilon^2$ of the KL-divergence ball. Furthermore, a suitable choice of $\epsilon$  in one region of the loss landscape may not be suitable for another. Hence, an adaptive scheme for choosing the radius of the KL-divergence ball could substantially enhance the performance of CoNES.”

**[Q.]** The paper cites [Salimans 2017] right next to [Rechenberg 1973]. Citing [Salimans 2017] as an original paper on ES reveals a serious lack of knowledge of the field. 

**[A.]** Throughout the paper, we cite [Salimans 2017] in the context of reinforcement learning (RL) and not as a pioneer of ES methods itself. This can particularly be noted in Section 2 (related work), where [Salimans 2017] is discussed under “Evolutionary strategies for reinforcement learning”. If there was an oversight anywhere in the paper where we implied that [Salimans 2017] was the progenitor of ES methods, we would be happy to fix it.

**[Q.]** It is claimed in the introduction that NES would need to estimate the Fisher matrix. That is wrong in many ways. First of all, Gaussian distributions are used all the time, and then the matrix is known in analytic form. Second, the xNES implementation of NES provides a neat way of getting around computing the matrix at all.

**[A.]** We are aware that NES can be computed analytically for Gaussian distributions; in fact, we ourselves analytically compute NES for the baseline in our numerical implementations, as mentioned in Section 7: “This family of belief distributions [Gaussian distributions] permits the implementation of NES exactly (i.e., without having to numerically estimate the Fisher information matrix (Sun et al., 2009)) for high-dimensional problems, serving as a strong baseline to compare CoNES against.” We would be happy to clarify this in the Introduction. However, we emphasize again that the primary contribution of CoNES is not its ability to circumvent estimation of the Fisher information matrix, but rather its ability to endow trust-region-like benefits to NES-like gradient estimates.

##### **Due to space limitation, the authors' response continues in the following comment**

content.title: Author Response: Part 2
content.comment:
**[Q.]** Section 4.2: "This gradient estimate is then supplied to a gradient-based optimizer to update the belief distribution." Wrong. All practical NES implementations rely on ranking of solutions, not on the plain gradient estimator. This is absolutely essential, see Beyer. "Convergence analysis of evolutionary algorithms that are based on the paradigm of information geometry." Evolutionary Computation 22.4 (2014): 679-709.

**[A.]** Our algorithm, and the others we implement in our paper **do** rank the solutions. In our code, please see the file `es_grad.py`; the results for ES are for `method=='centered_utility'` (line 33), the results for NES are for `method=='eNES_logvar_centered_utility'` (line 154), and the results for CoNES are for `method=='coNES_logvar_centered_utility'` (line 96). The suffix “centered_utility” refers to the employment of a rank-based utility scheme which is available as the function named `centered_utility` (line 22).

We would be happy to include a clarification (that we do perform ranking) in the paper and remove the methods from the code that we do not use in the results.

**[Q.]** the authors use bad initial parameters for their competitor methods on purpose

**[A.]** We used the same initial parameters for ES, NES, and CoNES. For CMA-ES, we used the default set of parameters as chosen by pycma, as was mentioned in Section 7.1: “Hyperparameters for ES, NES, and CoNES are shared across all problems (see Appendix B) while the hyperparameters of CMA are the default values chosen by PyCMA”.

**[Q.]** The only way to make a non-elitist ES like CMA-ES get worse on a convex function is to start it with a too large initial step size. This happens on all four analytic problems. It is well known that CMA-ES vastly outperforms NES on sphere due to better step size control. 

**[A.]** CMA-ES not outperforming (vanilla) ES on sphere has been observed in other papers as well; please see the first plot of Figure 4 in this paper: https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2019/file/88bade49e98db8790df275fcebb37a13-Paper.pdf.

**[Q.]** I checked the code. Whatever is referred to here as an ES or a NES algorithm has not much to do with it. I refuse to call these algorithms ES. There is no selection, there is not even any ranking. What I see here are cheaply estimated stochastic (natural) gradients at work. 

**[A.]** As we clarified earlier, we are ranking the solutions.

**[Q.]** Please ALWAYS plot objective function regrets and step sizes on a log-scale.

**[A.]** Figure 2 in the paper is a log-scale plot. We will update Figure 3 to be a log-scale plot as well.

content.title: Review Update
content.comment:
### Main Contribution
The main contribution is to have $\epsilon \gg 0$ in the natural gradient estimation. That makes sense to me, and I acknowledge that this contribution is valuable. Let me recommend to improve the presentation of the paper. The core contribution is not really made clear before arriving at section 5. There are various hints, but they remain vague and do not necessarily look like the main contribution.

### Citations
Thanks for clarifying the roles of the different citations. I have a problem with citing Salimans for pioneering ES for RL. Sure, it was an influential paper, but the main novelty was scaling to many cores. OpenAI were the first to train large networks with ES, that's all. ES were used for RL for a long time. For example, the following works seem relevant:
@inproceedings{igel2003neuroevolution,
  title={Neuroevolution for reinforcement learning using evolution strategies},
  author={Igel, Christian},
  booktitle={The 2003 Congress on Evolutionary Computation, 2003. CEC'03.},
  volume={4},
  pages={2588--2595},
  year={2003},
  organization={IEEE}
}
@article{heidrich2009neuroevolution,
  title={Neuroevolution strategies for episodic reinforcement learning},
  author={Heidrich-Meisner, Verena and Igel, Christian},
  journal={Journal of Algorithms},
  volume={64},
  number={4},
  pages={152--168},
  year={2009},
  publisher={Elsevier}
}
Also NES was applies to RL benchmarks, e.g., double pole balancing. Salimans et al. did not give proper credit. I am asking you to do better :)

### Ranking
I am glad that you are ranking solutions. Please make this clear explicitly. Similarly, equation (3) gives the main motivation for the NES proceeding, but all implementations use ranking. That's not just a detail, although it may seem like one at first.

### Experiments
Regarding the experiments, I stick to my assessment.

For CMA-ES on the sphere function, there are multiple effects. First of all, disabling covariance matrix adaptation increases the speed. That's trivial and uninteresting, because it happens only on this specific benchmark (and related highly symmetric problems rarely encountered in practice).

Everything else depends on step size adaptation. In the setting considered in the experiments the evaluation budget is relatively small compared to the problem dimension. Consequently, step size initialization dominates all other effects. The presented evaluation obviously starts with a too large step size. So what is compared is the ability of an algorithm to reduce its step size quickly. That has nothing to do with CoNES finding good optimization directions or not.

Generally speaking, CSA is not the best method in high dimensions (say, above 100 or a few 100) for adapting an initially wrong step size. PyCMA is simply not tuned for that case. In particular for a step size that is initially off, it may be better to use two-point adaptation. The simple 1/5-rule with large enough adaptation factors also works well. When running experiments for long enough (aiming at high solution precision), CSA may finally overtake.

For experiments in high dimensions with CMA-ES please try the following, in particular when insisting on using an initially too large step size: es = cma.CMAEvolutionStrategy(np.ones(1000), 1.0, {'AdaptSigma': cma.sigma_adaptation.CMAAdaptSigmaTPA}) Corresponding link to pycma: https://github.com/CMA-ES/pycma/blob/master/cma/sigma_adaptation.py

I subsume that you aim to prove that CoNES finds good optimization directions. In that regard, all methods should be equally good on the sphere. The best test would be to implement the different methods for finding a direction into the same code base, using the same step size adaptation. Once you have setup the experiments in such a way that everyone has the same performance on sphere (due to using the same step size control) then I am willing to look at differences on other functions. The current experiments do not even come close to answering the relevant research question.

content.title: Author Response
content.comment: We thank the reviewer for their constructive suggestions. We will update the manuscript in the next few days with better clarification of our contribution, the references raised by them, and their suggestions for the experiments.

content.title: Weak evaluation, limited novelty
content.review:
This paper proposes a variant of evolutionary strategies, which estimate a gradient of a black-box objective function by a limited number of Gaussian samples around the current search point. The proposed approaches replace the vanilla gradient with the natural gradient, the inverse Fisher information matrix times the vanilla gradient. Such an idea is introduced in natural evolution strategies (NES) and CMA-ES, where the inverse Fisher information matrix times the vanilla gradient can be computed directly (without computing the inverse Fisher information matrix). 

As I mentioned above, the multiplication of the inverse Fisher information matrix is known to be for free for Gaussian models. Indeed, different ES variants uses the natural gradient, such as eNES, xNES, CMA-ES, and their diagonal covariance matrix versions such as sep-CMA-ES and other covariance models such as R1-NES, VD-CMA. Strangely enough, the authors say in Section 5 that it is difficult to scale to very high-dimensional problems because the computational cost for the inversion of the Fisher information matrix, and they propose to use a numerical optimization to derive the natural gradient approximately. I couldn't find any reason why the authors prefer to numerically derive the natural gradient. I do not see much difference from separable-NES (JMLR 2014, 949-980), which uses the natural gradient and uses a diagonal covariance matrix. The separable-CMA-ES also compute the same. 

The authors compare the proposed approach with other ES variants. However, the authors didn't compare the performance with separable-NES nor separable-CMA-ES. What could be the possible reason that the proposed approach would be better than these approaches that compute the exact natural gradient on the same Gaussian models?

content.title: Author Response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their comments. Below we address the reviewer’s main comments:

**[Q.]** The proposed approaches replace the vanilla gradient with the natural gradient, the inverse Fisher information matrix times the vanilla gradient. Such an idea is introduced in natural evolution strategies (NES) and CMA-ES, where the inverse Fisher information matrix times the vanilla gradient can be computed directly (without computing the inverse Fisher information matrix). I couldn't find any reason why the authors prefer to numerically derive the natural gradient.

**[A.]** It is certainly true that one of the advantages of CoNES is its ability to circumvent computing the inverse of the Fisher information matrix, which the methods listed by the reviewer also permit. However, we emphasize that the primary advantage of CoNES lies in its ability to tune the direction of the estimated gradient with the step size of the optimizer, as mentioned in the Introduction of the paper: “tuning the radius of the KL-divergence ball facilitates better alignment of the update direction with the update step size, yielding faster convergence than NES (which provides the steepest ascent direction for infinitesimal step lengths).” We thus emphasize that CoNES should **not** be interpreted as a numerical approximation of the natural gradient. Instead, the primary benefit is the ability to tune the KL-divergence ball; this endows trust-region-like benefits to NES-like gradient estimates. The methods mentioned by the reviewer only provide estimates of the gradient for infinitesimal step lengths. 

Indeed, due to the importance of the radius of the KL-divergence ball, we provided a literature review on “Trust-regions for blackbox optimization” in Section 2, Related Work. 
We also raise this issue towards the end of Section 5: “The NES gradient is the sharpest ascent direction for an infinitesimal step size, but it may not be ideal for a larger step size. With CoNES, we can tune the scalar parameter $\epsilon$ to better align the update direction with the gradient-based optimizer’s step size (learning rate), yielding faster updates. Indeed, the choice of $\epsilon$ is important to the performance of CoNES as demonstrated in our numerical results in Section 7.2. The mechanism for selecting (or adapting) the hyperparameter $\epsilon$ is beyond the scope of this paper and will be explored in our future work.” 
In the results, we again point to the importance of the KL-divergence ball: “It is worth pointing out that for RL tasks, CoNES demonstrates high sensitivity to the choice of $\epsilon$. The results for CoNES reported in Fig. 4 and Table 1 are for the best choice of $\epsilon$ from $[\sqrt{0.1},\sqrt{1},\sqrt{10},\sqrt{100},\sqrt{1000}]$.” 
Finally, due to the importance of the choice of the KL-divergence ball’s radius, the first point we raise in our future work is: “The performance of CoNES is dependent on the choice of the radius $\epsilon^2$ of the KL-divergence ball. Furthermore, a suitable choice of $\epsilon$  in one region of the loss landscape may not be suitable for another. Hence, an adaptive scheme for choosing the radius of the KL-divergence ball could substantially enhance the performance of CoNES.”

**[Q.]** What could be the possible reason that the proposed approach would be better than these approaches that compute the exact natural gradient on the same Gaussian models?

**[A.]** In the paper, we compare our results against vanilla ES, NES, and CMA-ES (with default settings in pycma). For NES we compute the exact analytical inverse of the Fisher information matrix. Indeed, if our approach only returned an estimate of the natural gradient, then there is no reason to expect that our method would outperform NES. But, as we mentioned earlier, the primary benefit of CoNES is the ability to tune the radius of the KL-divergence ball on which CoNES is computed, allowing it to align the gradient estimate in accordance with the step size. This is, we believe, the primary reason behind the good performance of CoNES. It is also worth pointing out (as we noted in the results section) that the choice of the radius is crucial.
